extracted.intended_audience: readers of the Philosophical Transactions: natural philosophers and experimental practitioners (brewers, miners, physicians, instrument-makers)
extracted.subtask_description: Short reports of experimental methods, practical recipes, observational accounts, and engineering proposals in natural philosophy (17th‑century). Contains procedural instructions and empirical indicators for practice (e.g., malt-making, mine safety, burn treatments, microscopical observation, flying devices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Malt-making by covering in earth
rubrics_metrics.description: Lay the corn for malt all over the ground, cover it with 2–3 inches of earth (pared off and laid half one way and half the other), leave till the plot appears like a green field with sprouts within 10 or 14 days, then take up, shake earth from it and dry it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method ensures every good grain will grow and be mellow, floury, and sweet; beer made of it will be wholesome, pleasant, and of good brown colour. Note that malting this corn is little known among them and beer made of bread is more durable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Barley selection and storage for malt (Scotland)
rubrics_metrics.description: Malt is made only from barley; two-row barley makes the best malt though four-row is commonly used. Newly threshed barley makes better malt; barley threshed six weeks or more will not be good unless kept in equal temper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid keeping barley up against a wall (middle of heap freshest, outside/top over-dried, next to wall shoots, bottom rots). Best way to preserve threshed barley long is not to separate the chaff. Brewers keep barley in large rooms on boarded floors about a foot deep and turn it now and then with scoops. Barley overheated in stacks/barns before separation will never prove good for malt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steeping (infusion) criteria for barley
rubrics_metrics.description: Put barley into water and let it infuse till the water be of a bright reddish colour (about 3 days, variable with season, grain size, and weather).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know steeping sufficiency by colour of water and by other marks: excessive swelling indicates near-steep, over-steeped by too much softness; when in right temper it is like barley prepared to make broth. In summer malt seldom makes well; in winter steeping often needs longer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing the coming heap (germination control)
rubrics_metrics.description: After steeping drain 2–3 hours, turn with a scoop, and lay in a 'coming heap' about 20–24 inches deep where it lies ~40 hours (variable). Watch especially first 15–16 hours: roots begin to put forth; when roots have equally and fully appeared, within an hour turn the heap to prevent blades/spires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preventing blade/spire growth is essential — if allowed, the malt will be spoiled in taste and strength. If malt comes unevenly, turn so outermost lie inmost until all come alike. As soon as sufficiently come, spread to 5–6 inches and begin frequent turning (3–4 times), then once every 4–5 hours, thickening the heap by degrees for at least 48 hours. Frequent turning cools, dries, and 'deads' the grain making it mellow and separable from the husk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heating and drying (kiln) protocol for malt
rubrics_metrics.description: After heap management, throw up the malt into a high heap, let it lie till it grows as hot as the hand can endure (about 30 hours) to perfect sweetness and mellowness; then throw abroad to cool, turn again about 6–8 hours after, and dry it on the kiln with one fire (24 hours), then another more slow, and if need be a third.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If malt is not thoroughly dried it cannot be well ground nor dissolve well in brewing; ale will be red, bitter, and will not keep if drying is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fuel choice for kilning malt
rubrics_metrics.description: Best fuel for kiln is peat; next best is charcoal made of pit-coal or cinders; heath, broom, or furzes are bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If mixing fuels, burn the best first as it gives the strongest impression to taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventing spoilage in malt heaps (turning and heat control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn the coming heap frequently and regulate heap thickness; allow the heap to become hot enough to perfect sweetness but avoid conditions that make some grains shoot blades or overheat portions (middle warms first, outsides/at top over-dry, near wall may shoot, bottom may rot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent and staged turning (initially every few hours, later every 4–5 hours) and controlled piling over ~48 hours equalizes germination and prevents spoilage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of burns (folk/practical remedies)
rubrics_metrics.description: When burned (e.g., in mines), apply hot milk to bathe the burned places immediately and afterwards use an ointment proper for burns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Footnote guidance: In slight and partial burns, cold water applied before the skin blisters produces immediate good effect. For more violent and extensive burns, prevention of ulceration/sloughs/mortification is best achieved by applying spirit of wine, oil of turpentine, and other stimulants; common oily applications are improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mine-safety practice regarding fire-damp and lighting
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent mischief from fire-damps: keep the mine air very quick (well ventilated) and use no candles except single-wick candles of 60 or 70 to the pound; place candles behind the workers and never present them to the breast of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These single-wick candles give as great a light in those works as heavier candles do elsewhere; practice described as effective where fire-damps continually occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microscopical observation and quantitative extrapolation (Leuwenhoek)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe fluids (melt of fish, vasa deferentia, semen, testicle matter) with magnifying instruments to detect innumerable small animals; note motion (active or without motion) and morphology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate numbers by sampling and extrapolation: e.g., estimate how many 'sands' per inch (100 per inch), infer number of 'sand'-sized sample volumes per cubic inch (~3,000,000), count animals in a sample sand-sized quantity (e.g., 10,000), and scale up to entire volume (e.g., melt of codfish) to estimate total numbers. Be aware such numerical extrapolations and biological interpretations (role in generation) can be highly speculative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical testing and staged trials for flying apparatus (Sieur Besnier)
rubrics_metrics.description: Flying-engine consists of four folding wings moved by arms and legs via strings; to attempt flying, fit poles on shoulders and move wings in alternating diagonal sequence; begin trials by springing from a stool, then table, higher windows, and gradually from a garret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two principal needs: (1) a substance exceedingly light and of great extension to suspend weight of man; (2) a tail to help support and steer. The author concedes he cannot raise himself from earth or sustain flight long because of lack of strength and quickness in arms/legs; expects short glides from elevated places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design principles for a lighter-than-air 'flying ship' (Francesco Lana)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume air has weight and that a vessel from which air is evacuated (or largely evacuated) and whose shell weighs less than the weight of air displaced will ascend; propose method to evacuate large vessels via a pipe and stopcock by filling with water, inverting, draining, then closing to leave a near-evacuated space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use geometrical demonstration and weight calculations (example: brass vessel of diameter 14 ft with thin plate weighing 3 oz per square foot — total shell vs contained air weight computed) to show net lifting capability; increase bulk without increasing plate thickness to carry additional weight. (Note: author uses experimental weighing method to estimate relative weight of air to water; modern values differ.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational method for lunar occultation (astronomical measurement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe occultations (e.g., Jupiter by the Moon) under clear sky and in presence of colleagues to measure planetary apparent diameters and path relative to lunar features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lunar spots and careful timing/position measurement to measure apparent diameter; repeated long-term observation experience (e.g., 50 years) improves accuracy.
